stem: An agent is configured to always call at least three tools for every request, regardless of content, as a blanket policy. What is the most likely downside of this policy for simple, self-contained requests?

options.text: Unnecessary added latency and complexity with no corresponding benefit for requests that didn't need any tool at all
Guaranteed improvement in accuracy for every single request
The complete elimination of all possible errors
No downside whatsoever under any circumstances

explanation.why_correct: For simple, self-contained requests that don't actually need external information or actions, forcing multiple tool calls anyway adds latency and complexity without providing any real accuracy or correctness benefit.

why_incorrect.B: Calling tools unnecessarily does not inherently improve accuracy on tasks that were already well within the model's reliable knowledge.
why_incorrect.C: Blanket tool-calling does not eliminate all possible errors; a tool call itself can also return incorrect information or be misapplied.
why_incorrect.D: There is a real, meaningful downside (wasted latency/complexity) for tasks that didn't actually need tool use.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Blanket, content-independent tool-calling policies waste resources on tasks that don't need tools, without a compensating accuracy benefit.

stem: Which pair of tool categories reflects the key distinction discussed between types of tools an agent might use?

options.text: Tools invented before 2020 versus tools invented after 2020
Tools written in Python versus tools written in any other language
Tools that are free versus tools that cost money to use
Information-retrieval tools (read-only) versus action tools (cause real side effects)

explanation.why_correct: The key conceptual distinction discussed is between read-only, information-retrieval tools and action tools that cause real, persistent external side effects -- this distinction drives differences in appropriate caution.

why_incorrect.B: The programming language used to implement a tool has no bearing on the conceptual read-only versus side-effecting distinction that matters for risk assessment.
why_incorrect.C: Cost is a separate, unrelated practical consideration from the fundamental risk distinction between information retrieval and real-world action.
why_incorrect.A: The date a tool was created has no bearing on whether it is read-only or side-effecting.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: The key tool-risk distinction is read-only information retrieval versus side-effecting real-world action, not implementation details like language, cost, or age.

stem: Which of the following are genuine capabilities that tools add to an otherwise tool-less language model? (Select 3)

options.text: Access to information that changed or emerged after the model's training cutoff
The ability to cause real, persistent side effects in external systems
The ability to verify claims against a traceable external source
The ability to generate grammatically correct sentences

explanation.why_correct: Tools specifically add access to post-training information, the ability to cause real external side effects, and traceable verification against external sources -- capabilities a tool-less model lacks natively.

why_incorrect.D: Generating grammatically correct sentences is a native language-modeling capability that does not depend on tool use at all.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Tools add fresh information access, real-world action capability, and traceable verification -- not basic language generation, which models already do natively.
